exercises.title: Stating Gershgorin discs
exercises.description: State the Gershgorin discs of $A = \begin{pmatrix}4&1&0\\1&3&1\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and conclude a region containing all eigenvalues.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Centre $a_{ii}$, radius = sum of the magnitudes of the other entries of row $i$.

Step 2: Discs
$K_1$: centre $4$, radius $1$. $K_2$: centre $3$, radius $1 + 1 = 2$. $K_3$: centre $2$, radius $1$.

Step 3: Union
$K_1 = [3,5]$, $K_2 = [1,5]$, $K_3 = [1,3]$ (real due to symmetry). All eigenvalues lie in $[1,5]$.

Step 4: Check
Actual eigenvalues $1.268,\ 3,\ 4.732$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Rows, not columns: the radius comes from the other entries of the same row.

exercises.title: Two power method steps
exercises.description: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ with $v_0 = (1,1)^T$ perform two steps of the power method (normalising in the Euclidean norm).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$w = Av$, $v \leftarrow w/\|w\|_2$.

Step 4: Eigenvalue estimate
Factor $\|Av_1\| = 3.6056 \approx \lambda_1$ (for normalised $v_1$ we have $\|Av\| \to |\lambda_1|$).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Normalise in every step! Without normalisation $\|v\|$ grows like $\lambda_1^k$.

exercises.title: Computing a Rayleigh quotient
exercises.description: Compute the Rayleigh quotient of $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ for $v = (1,2)^T$ and compare with $\lambda_1 = 3.618$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$R(v) = \dfrac{v^TAv}{v^Tv}$.

Step 3: Denominator and quotient
$v^Tv = 1 + 4 = 5$, $R = 18/5 = 3.6$.

Step 4: Comparison
Error $3.618 - 3.6 = 0.018$ ($0.5\%$) – although $v$ is only rough: the angle to $(0.526, 0.851)$ is $5°$. That is the square (quadratic accuracy).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Always divide by $v^Tv$ if $v$ is not normalised.

exercises.title: Convergence factor
exercises.description: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ determine the convergence factor $|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|$ of the power method and the number of steps for a reduction by $10^{-3}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Eigenvalues: $\lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 5 = 0$.

Step 2: Eigenvalues
$\lambda_{1,2} = \frac{5 \pm\sqrt5}{2} = 3.618,\ 1.382$.

Step 3: Factor
$\left|\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right| = \frac{1.382}{3.618} = 0.382$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Factor $\ll 1$ ⇒ fast; factor near $1$ ⇒ power method unsuitable.

exercises.title: Exact 2×2 eigenvalues
exercises.description: Determine the eigenvalues of $A = \begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$ exactly and check that the power method with $v_0 = (1,1)$ immediately finds the largest.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$\det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 - \mathrm{tr}\,\lambda + \det = 0$.

Step 2: Polynomial
$\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = 5$ or $2$.

Step 3: Power method
$A(1,1)^T = (5, 5)^T = 5\cdot(1,1)^T$: $v_0$ is already an eigenvector for $\lambda = 5$ – a stroke of luck.

Step 4: Gershgorin
Discs: centre $4$ radius $1$, centre $3$ radius $2$: eigenvalues in $[1, 5]$ ✓ ($2$ and $5$).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Trace $= \lambda_1 + \lambda_2$, determinant $= \lambda_1\lambda_2$: quick check for $2\times2$.

exercises.title: Choosing a shift
exercises.description: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ (eigenvalues $1.382$, $3.618$) inverse iteration should find the smaller eigenvalue. Compare the convergence factors for $\mu = 0$ and $\mu = 1.5$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Eigenvalues of $(A - \mu I)^{-1}$: $\frac{1}{\lambda_i - \mu}$; factor = quotient of the two magnitudes.

Step 4: Consequence
With the shift convergence becomes $7\times$ faster per step ($0.056$ versus $0.382$).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The shift $\mu$ should be closer to the wanted eigenvalue than to all others.

exercises.title: Invertibility from Gershgorin
exercises.description: Use Gershgorin to justify that $B = \begin{pmatrix}5&1&1\\1&6&2\\0&1&4\end{pmatrix}$ is invertible.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$B$ is invertible exactly when $0$ is not an eigenvalue.

Step 2: Discs
Centre $5$, radius $2$: $[3,7]$. Centre $6$, radius $3$: $[3,9]$. Centre $4$, radius $1$: $[3,5]$.

Step 3: Conclusion
All discs lie to the right of $3$, $0$ is in none. So $0$ is not an eigenvalue and $B$ is invertible; even all eigenvalues have $\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda \ge 3$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Gershgorin is the proof behind “strictly diagonally dominant matrices are nonsingular”.

exercises.title: Estimating the spectral radius
exercises.description: Estimate $\rho(B)$ for the same matrix $B$ with Gershgorin and compare with the actual value $7.21$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$\rho(B) \le \max_i(|b_{ii}| + r_i)$ (outermost edge of the discs).

Step 3: Columns
Column discs: $5 \pm 1$, $6 \pm 2$, $4 \pm 3$: $\max = 8$ (column sum $\|B\|_1 = \max(6, 8, 7)$). Combined: $\rho(B) \le 8$ – sharper.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
At the same time $\rho(B) \le \|B\|_\infty = 9$ and $\le \|B\|_1 = 8$ – every norm yields a bound (4.4).

exercises.title: Inverse iteration with shift
exercises.description: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ with $\mu = 1.5$, $v_0 = (1,1)^T$ perform two steps of inverse iteration and compute the Rayleigh quotients.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Solve $(A - 1.5I)x = v$ with $A - 1.5I = \begin{pmatrix}0.5&1\\1&1.5\end{pmatrix}$, $\det = -0.25$.

Step 4: Comparison
Exact $\lambda_2 = 1.381966$: error after step 2: $3\cdot10^{-4}$. One more step: $R = 1.381967$, then $1.381966015$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
One linear system per step (with the same decomposition!). With the shift the eigenvalue is accurate to $3$ digits after 2 steps.

exercises.title: Power method with shift
exercises.description: Show that the power method applied to $B = A - 1.5I$ (instead of $A$) for $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ finds the eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ much faster and perform two steps.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Eigenvalues of $B$: $\lambda_i - 1.5$; factor $\left|\frac{\lambda_2 - 1.5}{\lambda_1 - 1.5}\right|$.

Step 2: Factor
$\lambda(B) = 2.118$ and $-0.118$: factor $\frac{0.118}{2.118} = 0.056$ instead of $0.382$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
A clever shift also accelerates the plain power method – without a linear system. Ideal: $\mu = \frac{\lambda_2 + \lambda_n}{2}$ (“optimal shift”).

exercises.title: One QR step (2×2)
exercises.description: For $A_0 = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ perform one step of the QR algorithm ($A_0 = Q_0R_0$, $A_1 = R_0Q_0$) and check trace and determinant.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Gram–Schmidt on the columns $a_1 = (2,1)$, $a_2 = (1,3)$.

Step 3: RQ
$A_1 = R_0Q_0 = \sqrt5\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt5}\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 4: Check
Trace $3 + 2 = 5$ ✓, $\det = 6 - 1 = 5$ ✓ – same as $A_0$. Diagonal $(3, 2)$: first approximation to $(3.618, 1.382)$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
$A_1 = Q_0^TA_0Q_0$ is similar to $A_0$ ⇒ the same eigenvalues.

exercises.title: Gershgorin: rows and columns
exercises.description: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}4&2&0\\0&3&0.5\\1&0&2\end{pmatrix}$ determine row and column discs and the region containing all eigenvalues. (Eigenvalues: $4.32,\ 2.34 \pm 0.56i$.)
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The eigenvalues of $A$ and $A^T$ agree: one may use row OR column discs – and intersect both results.

Step 2: Row discs
$K_1$: centre $4$, $r = 2$; $K_2$: centre $3$, $r = 0.5$; $K_3$: centre $2$, $r = 1$. Union: discs around $4$ (radius $2$), $3$ (radius $0.5$), $2$ (radius $1$) – real part $[1, 6]$.

Step 3: Column discs
Column 1: $|0| + |1| = 1$ around $4$; column 2: $|2| + |0| = 2$ around $3$; column 3: $|0| + |0.5| = 0.5$ around $2$. Real part: $[3,5] \cup [1,5] \cup [1.5,2.5] = [1,5]$.

Step 4: Intersection
All eigenvalues have $\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda \in [1, 5]$ – sharper than $[1,6]$. Check: $4.32,\ 2.34 \pm 0.56i$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Combine the row and column versions: often much sharper bounds for non-symmetric matrices.

exercises.title: Number of steps for accuracy
exercises.description: How many steps does the power method need for $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ so that (a) the eigenvector, (b) the Rayleigh quotient is accurate to $10^{-6}$?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Vector error $\sim 0.382^k$, Rayleigh error $\sim 0.382^{2k} = 0.146^k$.

Step 4: Check
From the table: at $k = 5$ the Rayleigh error is $8\cdot10^{-6}$; each step multiplies by $0.146$, so about $2\cdot10^{-7}$ at $k = 7$ and $2.5\cdot10^{-8}$ at $k = 8$ – below $10^{-6}$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The Rayleigh quotient needs about half as many steps as the eigenvector (for symmetric $A$).

exercises.title: Rayleigh accuracy versus vector accuracy
exercises.description: For $v_1 = (0.6, 0.8)^T$ the angle to the eigenvector $(0.5257, 0.8507)$ is about $5.15°$. Compare the relative vector error with the relative error of the Rayleigh quotient.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Angle in radians $\theta = 0.0899$; Rayleigh error $\approx(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)\sin^2\theta$.

Step 2: Vector error
$\|v_1 - u_1\| \approx \theta = 0.0899$ – about $9\%$.

Step 4: Conclusion
$9\%$ vector error ⇒ $0.5\%$ eigenvalue error: quadratic ($0.09^2 = 0.008$, times a constant).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
This holds only for symmetric (or normal) matrices. For non-symmetric $A$ the error is only linear.

exercises.title: Normalising the eigenvector
exercises.description: From the power method $v_3 \propto (7, 11)^T$ is given. Normalise to length $1$ and compare with the exact eigenvector $(1, \frac{1 + \sqrt5}{2})/\|\cdot\|$ for $\lambda_1$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Length $\|(7,11)\| = \sqrt{49 + 121} = \sqrt{170}$.

Step 4: Error
Difference $(0.0112, -0.0070)$, norm $0.0132$ (about $1.3\%$).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Eigenvectors are determined only up to a factor (including sign) – normalise and choose the sign consistently.

exercises.title: Power method for |λ₁| = |λ₂|
exercises.description: Show that the power method for $A = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ with $v_0 = (1,0)^T$ does not converge and remedy this with a shift.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Eigenvalues $\pm1$ with equal magnitude.

Step 2: Behaviour
$Av_0 = (0,1) = v_1$, $Av_1 = (1,0) = v_0$: the sequence oscillates between $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ and does not converge. The Rayleigh quotient is always $0$ (wrong, $\lambda = \pm1$).

Step 3: Shift
$B = A + I = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $2$ and $0$. Factor $0/2 = 0$: $Bv_0 = (1,1)$ is already an eigenvector for $2$, hence for $A$ with eigenvalue $2 - 1 = 1$.

Step 4: Remember
A shift makes the magnitudes different: $|\lambda_1 + \mu| \ne |\lambda_2 + \mu|$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The power method needs a unique eigenvalue of largest magnitude (a dominant eigenvalue).

exercises.title: Proving convergence of the power method
exercises.description: Let $A$ be diagonalisable with eigenvalues $|\lambda_1| > |\lambda_2| \ge \dots \ge |\lambda_n|$ and eigenvectors $u_i$; $v_0 = \sum c_iu_i$ with $c_1 \ne 0$. Show that $A^kv_0/\|A^kv_0\|$ converges to $\pm u_1$ (up to scaling) with rate $|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Let powers of $A$ act on the eigenbasis and factor out $\lambda_1^k$.

Step 2: Expansion
$A^kv_0 = \sum_ic_i\lambda_i^ku_i = \lambda_1^k\Bigl(c_1u_1 + \sum_{i\ge2}c_i\bigl(\tfrac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_1}\bigr)^ku_i\Bigr)$.

Step 3: Estimate
The sum is $O(|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|^k)$ since $|\lambda_i/\lambda_1| \le |\lambda_2/\lambda_1| < 1$. So $A^kv_0 = \lambda_1^k\bigl(c_1u_1 + O(\rho^k)\bigr)$ with $\rho = |\lambda_2/\lambda_1|$.

Step 4: Normalising
After normalisation $v_k$ points in direction $\mathrm{sign}(\lambda_1)^kc_1u_1 + O(\rho^k)$: convergence of the direction (up to sign) with rate $\rho$.

Step 5: Rayleigh
$R(v_k) = \lambda_1 + O(\rho^k)$ in general, $O(\rho^{2k})$ for symmetric $A$ (angle squared).

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Conditions: dominant eigenvalue and $c_1 \ne 0$. In rounding arithmetic $c_1 \ne 0$ creeps in by itself.

exercises.title: Proving Gershgorin
exercises.description: Prove: if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ with eigenvector $x$, then $\lambda \in K_i$ for some $i$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Choose the component of $x$ with the largest magnitude.

Step 2: Setup
Let $|x_i| = \|x\|_\infty > 0$. The $i$-th equation of $Ax = \lambda x$: $\sum_ja_{ij}x_j = \lambda x_i$.

Step 3: Rearranging
$(\lambda - a_{ii})x_i = \sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}x_j$.

Step 4: Estimating
$|\lambda - a_{ii}||x_i| \le \sum_{j
e i}|a_{ij}||x_j| \le \sum_{j
e i}|a_{ij}|\cdot|x_i|$. Dividing by $|x_i| 
e 0$: $|\lambda - a_{ii}| \le \sum_{j
e i}|a_{ij}| = r_i$.

Step 5: Consequence
So $\lambda \in K_i$. Example $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ with $\lambda = 3.618$, $x = (0.526, 0.851)$: largest component $i = 2$: $|3.618 - 3| = 0.618 \le 1$ ✓.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
There is no statement about which eigenvalue lies in which disc – only: every eigenvalue lies in the union. (Disjoint groups of discs contain exactly as many eigenvalues as discs.)

exercises.title: QR iteration preserves eigenvalues
exercises.description: Show $A_{k+1} = Q_k^TA_kQ_k$ and conclude that $A_k$ and $A_0$ have the same eigenvalues. Check trace and determinant for $A_0, A_1, A_2$ of the example ($A_2 = \begin{pmatrix}3.5&0.5\\0.5&1.5\end{pmatrix}$).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$A_k = Q_kR_k \Rightarrow R_k = Q_k^TA_k$.

Step 2: Similarity
$A_{k+1} = R_kQ_k = (Q_k^TA_k)Q_k = Q_k^TA_kQ_k$ – a similarity transformation with orthogonal $Q_k$.

Step 3: Eigenvalues
Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial: $\det(Q^TAQ - \lambda I) = \det(Q^T(A - \lambda I)Q) = \det(A - \lambda I)$.

Step 4: Numbers
$A_0$: trace $5$, $\det = 5$. $A_1 = \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$: $5$, $5$. $A_2$: trace $5$, $\det = 5.25 - 0.25 = 5$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Orthogonal similarity is numerically stable – that is why QR is the standard. Symmetry is also preserved.

exercises.title: Rayleigh quotient iteration
exercises.description: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ with $v_0 = (1,1)^T$ perform the Rayleigh quotient iteration ($\mu_k = R(v_k)$, $(A - \mu_kI)x = v_k$) and observe the speed of convergence.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The shift is updated in every step – hence cubic convergence.

Step 2: Step 0
$\mu_0 = R(v_0) = 3.5$. $A - 3.5I = \begin{pmatrix}-1.5&1\\1&-0.5\end{pmatrix}$, inverse $\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\4&6\end{pmatrix}$. $x_1 = (6, 10)$, $v_1 = (0.5145, 0.8575)$.

Step 5: Order
Errors: $1.8\cdot10^{-1},\ 3.9\cdot10^{-4},\ 4\cdot10^{-9},\ <10^{-12}$: each roughly the cube of the previous – cubic.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Price: new decomposition in every step; an almost singular $A - \mu I$ does no harm because the error lies in the direction of the eigenvector.

exercises.title: Deflation
exercises.description: Suppose $\lambda_1 = 3.618$ with normalised eigenvector $q_1 = (0.5257, 0.8507)^T$ of $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ has been found. Show that $A' = A - \lambda_1q_1q_1^T$ has the eigenvalues $0$ and $\lambda_2$ and compute $A'$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Symmetric $A$ has orthonormal eigenvectors: $A = \lambda_1q_1q_1^T + \lambda_2q_2q_2^T$.

Step 2: Eigenvalues of A'
$A'q_1 = Aq_1 - \lambda_1q_1(q_1^Tq_1) = \lambda_1q_1 - \lambda_1q_1 = 0$; $A'q_2 = Aq_2 - \lambda_1q_1(q_1^Tq_2) = \lambda_2q_2 - 0$.

Step 3: Numerical values
$q_1q_1^T = \begin{pmatrix}0.2764&0.4472\\0.4472&0.7236\end{pmatrix}$, times $3.618$: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1.618\\1.618&2.618\end{pmatrix}$. $A' = \begin{pmatrix}1&-0.618\\-0.618&0.382\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 4: Check
Trace $A' = 1.382 = \lambda_2$ ✓, $\det A' = 0.382 - 0.382 = 0$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
On $A'$ the power method now gives the second-largest eigenvalue. In practice (rounding errors) one deflates with care – or better via Hessenberg/QR.

exercises.title: Conditioning of eigenvalues
exercises.description: For symmetric $A$ we have $|\tilde\lambda - \lambda| \le \|E\|_2$ under the perturbation $A + E$. Show with $A = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $E = \begin{pmatrix}0&0\\\varepsilon&0\end{pmatrix}$ that this fails for non-symmetric matrices.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$A$ has the double eigenvalue $1$ (Jordan block). Compute the perturbation.

Step 2: Perturbed polynomial
$A + E = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\\varepsilon&1\end{pmatrix}$: $(1 - \lambda)^2 - \varepsilon = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = 1\pm\sqrt\varepsilon$.

Step 3: Numbers
$\varepsilon = 10^{-8}$: eigenvalue shift $\sqrt\varepsilon = 10^{-4}$ – $10^4$ times the perturbation $\|E\| = 10^{-8}$.

Step 4: Reason
Bauer–Fike: $|\tilde\lambda - \lambda| \le \kappa(V)\|E\|$ with the condition number of the eigenvector matrix $V$. Symmetric: $\kappa(V) = 1$. For the Jordan block $V$ is not even invertible ($\kappa = \infty$).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Eigenvalues of symmetric matrices are perfectly conditioned; for non-normal matrices the condition can be huge (cf. Wilkinson polynomial, 4.2).

exercises.title: PageRank as a power method
exercises.description: Three web pages: A links to B and C, B to C, C to A. The (column-stochastic) transition matrix is $M = \begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\\frac12&0&0\\\frac12&1&0\end{pmatrix}$. The PageRank is the eigenvector for $\lambda = 1$. Determine it directly and with the power method ($x_0 = (\frac13,\frac13,\frac13)$, a few steps).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$Mx = x$ with $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 1$.

Step 4: Convergence rate
The other eigenvalues are $-\frac12\pm\frac12i$ with magnitude $\frac{1}{\sqrt2} = 0.707$. Error per step $\times0.707$; after $12$ steps $\approx 0.707^{12} = 0.016$ (observed $0.001$–$0.002$).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The real PageRank mixes in a “random surfer”: $G = 0.85M + 0.15\cdot\frac1n\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T$ – the second eigenvalue is then $\le 0.85$, convergence is guaranteed.

exercises.title: Hessenberg form (3×3)
exercises.description: Bring $A = \begin{pmatrix}4&1&2\\2&3&1\\2&1&5\end{pmatrix}$ to Hessenberg form by a Givens similarity $G\,A\,G^T$ (rotation in rows/columns $2,3$) and check the trace.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Goal: $a_{31} = 0$. Rotate $(a_{21}, a_{31}) = (2, 2)$: $c = s = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$.

Step 2: Rotation
$G = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&c&s\\0&-s&c\end{pmatrix}$ with $c = s = 0.7071$.

Step 4: GAGᵀ
Rotate columns $2,3$ with $G^T$: $H = \begin{pmatrix}4&2.121&0.707\\2.828&5&1\\0&1&3\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 5: Check
Trace $4 + 5 + 3 = 12$ ✓ $= 4 + 3 + 5$. The eigenvalues $7.236,\ 2.764,\ 2$ are unchanged (checked via the characteristic polynomial).

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Hessenberg: a QR step costs only $O(n^2)$; for symmetric $A$ the matrix $H$ becomes tridiagonal.
